headline: Forests are not just collections of trees—they're connected communities that communicate
universal_truth: What looks like individuals may actually be a networked community
fun_facts: Trees communicate through underground fungal networks—nicknamed the 'wood wide web'
Mother trees send nutrients to their seedlings through fungal connections
A single teaspoon of forest soil contains more organisms than people on Earth
discussion_questions: What invisible networks connect you to others?
How does knowing forests communicate change how you see them?
What 'nutrients' do you share with your community?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: A forest looks like a crowd of separate trees competing for light. But beneath the soil, something extraordinary is happening. Trees are connected by vast fungal networks, sharing resources, sending warnings, nurturing their young. A forest is a single superorganism.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: How do trees—rooted in place, unable to move or speak—communicate with each other? What possible mechanism could connect organisms that seem so isolated?

options.text: Through fungal networks in the soil that connect their root systems
options.response: Yes. Fungi create underground highways that transfer nutrients, water, and chemical signals between trees.

options.text: By releasing chemical signals into the air
options.response: Trees do release airborne chemicals, but the main network is underground...

q1.title: The Wood Wide Web
q1.script: Beneath every forest is a vast fungal network—mycorrhizae—connecting tree roots. Trees exchange carbon, nitrogen, water, and even chemical warning signals through these networks. A tree being attacked by insects can warn its neighbors through fungal messages.
q1.prompt: What's your first impression of "The Wood Wide Web"?

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Mother Trees
q2.script: Large, old trees—called mother trees—recognize their own seedlings and preferentially send them nutrients through fungal networks. They reduce their own root competition near their offspring. Trees practice parenting we never knew existed.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: Soil Abundance
q3.script: A single teaspoon of forest soil contains more living organisms than all humans on Earth—bacteria, fungi, nematodes, and more. The forest floor is the planet's densest ecosystem. Most of the forest's life is invisible.
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: What looks like competition may be cooperation. What looks like isolation may be connection. The trees remind us that we too are part of networks we cannot see—connected in ways we're only beginning to understand.
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 59—the last day of February! Tomorrow begins March as we explore why jungles are so alive. Until then, walk through a forest and imagine the conversations happening underground.
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Hidden Networks - Map Your Connections
growTrack.learning_objective: Recognize the invisible networks you're part of
growTrack.activity: Sketch your 'wood wide web'—the visible and invisible connections that sustain you. Include people, organizations, ideas, and resources that feed you in ways you might not normally notice. Who are your 'mother trees'? Who do you nurture?
